name: Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis)
populations: people in repetitive-gripping or vibrating-tool work
summary: Painful catching or locking of a finger or thumb because a thickened flexor tendon and A1 pulley no longer glide smoothly. Common in women, people with diabetes and repetitive gripping work.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Orthosis, injection or both gave resolution or improvement in 68.9% of 104 people in one trial; pooled injection success was 57% across four older RCTs

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Active composite fist with palpation of a tender A1 pulley nodule; grade with the Quinnell classification (grades 1–4)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed for a typical presentation; ultrasound-guided and blind injections did not differ significantly in a systematic review

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age 52–62 years in injection trials, with about 75% women

keyFacts.label: Risk setting
keyFacts.value: Diabetes: odds ratio 3.79 for trigger finger in a meta-analysis

overview:
Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosynovitis) is painful catching or locking of a finger or thumb as it bends or straightens. The flexor tendon cannot glide smoothly through the tight first annular (A1) pulley at the base of the digit, which is the site of triggering in nearly all cases [r1]. In a histological study of 104 trigger digits, the avascular, cartilage-like gliding surface of the A1 pulley became fissured and thin and was replaced by fibrous tissue and invading blood vessels as severity increased. These changes were characteristic and not related to inflammation [r2]. A lifetime incidence of 2–3% has been reported [r3].

Treatment is stepped: education and activity change, then a splint or corticosteroid injection, then release of the A1 pulley if triggering persists. The Cochrane review found only two small, poor-quality trials, in which corticosteroid with lidocaine beat lidocaine alone at four weeks [r4]. A later best-evidence synthesis found moderate evidence for injection in the very short term [r5]. Evidence for physiotherapy-led interventions (orthoses, exercise, shockwave) is limited and mostly from small trials [r6,r7,r8].

epidemiology.text:
A systematic review of four RCTs of corticosteroid injection found that 75% of the people studied were women, with average ages between 52 and 62 years [r9]. A lifetime incidence of 2–3% has been reported [r3]. In a Japanese series of 715 treated fingers, the middle finger was the most common (243 fingers), followed by the thumb (175) and the ring finger (155), and people had a mean of 1.9 affected fingers each, so multiple digits are common [r3].

Diabetes is the best-documented medical association. A meta-analysis of metabolic disorders and tendinopathy reported an odds ratio of 3.79 (95% CI 1.87–7.65) for trigger finger in people with diabetes, and diabetic women had a greater prevalence than diabetic men [r10]. Work factors also matter. In a Swedish cohort, 'much' exposure to vibrating hand-held tools was independently associated with trigger finger in women (hazard ratio 2.73, 95% CI 1.49–4.99) [r11], and trigger finger is described in jobs that need repetitive gripping [r12]. Hand dominance is often cited as a risk factor in clinical teaching, but none of the sources retrieved for this page reported it, so no figure is quoted.

intrinsic: Female sex: about 75% of participants in four injection RCTs were women [r9]
Age in the 50s and 60s: average ages were 52–62 years in those trials [r9]
Diabetes mellitus: odds ratio 3.79 for trigger finger in a meta-analysis [r10]
Diabetic complications (nephropathy and neuropathy) were associated with needing surgery after injection (prognostic marker, small trial) [r13]
Having more than one affected digit is common (mean 1.9 fingers per person in one series) [r3]
extrinsic: Heavy exposure to vibrating hand-held tools, in women (hazard ratio 2.73) [r11]
Sustained tool grip with a narrow handle or a tight pinch (clinical reasoning)
Sudden increase in gripping load, for example a new job or hobby (clinical)

mechanism.summary: There is no single injury moment. Repeated or sustained forceful gripping presses the flexor tendons against the A1 pulley at the distal palmar crease, over the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint (clinical). Over time the pulley's gliding surface wears and is replaced by fibrous tissue [r2], and the flexor tendon develops a nodule or thickened segment, so the tendon and its tunnel no longer match in size. The nodule catches as it passes under the pulley when the digit flexes and again when it extends [r1].
sequence: The hand grips a tool, handle or load with the MCP joint flexed, so the FDS and FDP tendons press volarly against the A1 pulley (clinical).
Repeated loading is proposed to raise mechanical stress on the pulley's fibrocartilaginous gliding surface [r2].
The gliding surface fissures and thins and is replaced by fibrous tissue, with vascular hyperplasia invading from the outer layer. These changes are not inflammatory [r2].

The pulley thickens and the flexor tendon forms a nodule, so the tunnel becomes too small for the tendon (clinical). In one RCT both A1 pulley and flexor tendon thickness were measured, and both fell after steroid injection [r14].
As the digit flexes, the nodule passes under the pulley and clicks or snaps. Tenderness over the A1 pulley is the earliest sign, followed by snapping without locking [r3].
If the nodule cannot pass back under the pulley, the digit locks in flexion and the patient must free it with the other hand (snapping with locking) [r3].
Long-standing disease can leave a fixed joint contracture, usually of the PIP joint (Quinnell grade 4) [r3].

variants.name: Trigger thumb in adults
variants.description: The flexor pollicis longus catches at the A1 pulley at the thumb MCP joint. The radial digital nerve lies directly over the thumb A1 pulley, so it must be identified and protected in any release [r1].

variants.name: Paediatric trigger thumb
variants.description: In a Hong Kong case series of 180 children, the mean age of onset was 19 months, and a nodule and a fixed flexion deformity were very common findings [r15].

variants.name: Diabetes-associated trigger finger
variants.description: Diabetes raises the risk of trigger finger [r10]. One RCT found injection less effective in diabetic than non-diabetic digits [r13], whereas a large claims analysis found similar success rates [r16].

variants.name: Occupational and vibration-related
variants.description: Heavy hand-held vibrating tool use was independently associated with trigger finger in women [r11], and repetitive gripping work is a recognised setting [r12].

variants.name: Triggering away from the A1 pulley
variants.description: The A1 pulley is the site of triggering in nearly all cases. Rarer sites include the A2 pulley, the A3 pulley and the palmar aponeurosis [r1].

anatomy.text: The flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) and flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendons run together in a fibro-osseous flexor sheath on the palmar side of each finger. Annular pulleys hold the tendons close to the phalanges. The A1 pulley, the first and most proximal, lies over the MCP joint at the distal palmar crease, and the A2 pulley covers the proximal phalanx. A normal A1 pulley has three layers: an inner, avascular gliding layer containing cartilage-like cells; an avascular middle layer of spindle-shaped fibroblasts; and an outer, richly vascularised layer that is continuous with the membranous tendon sheath [r2]. The palmar digital nerves run on each side of the finger, and at the thumb the radial digital nerve crosses directly over the A1 pulley [r1].

structures.name: A1 pulley
structures.role: The first annular pulley over the MCP joint. It keeps the flexor tendons against the metacarpal head, and it is the usual site of triggering [r1]. Its inner layer is a cartilage-like gliding surface [r2].

structures.name: Flexor tendon sheath
structures.role: Fibro-osseous tunnel, lined by synovium, that nourishes and guides the FDS and FDP tendons

structures.name: FDS and FDP tendons
structures.role: FDS flexes the PIP joint and FDP flexes the DIP joint; both help flex the MCP joint and finger grip. A nodule on either tendon can catch at the pulley (clinical).

structures.name: A2 pulley
structures.role: Long pulley over the proximal phalanx. It prevents bowstringing; full release should be avoided because it may cause bowstringing and flexion weakness [r1].

structures.name: Palmar digital nerves
structures.role: Sensory nerves that run beside the sheath. The radial digital nerve crosses the thumb A1 pulley and is at risk during release [r1].

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Trigger finger is a size mismatch between the flexor tendon and the A1 pulley tunnel. In the pulley, the histological changes are characteristic. The fibrocartilaginous gliding surface becomes fissured and thin, then discontinuous or even destroyed, while vascular hyperplasia from the outer layer becomes excessive and reaches the synovial space of the sheath. The severity of these changes correlated with the clinical severity (p < .001). The authors judged that the changes were not related to inflammation and may reflect an increase in mechanical stress along the flexor tendons [r2].

The tendon itself also thickens. In an RCT of 92 people, A1 pulley thickness and flexor tendon thickness were measured at the affected site, and both decreased more after steroid injection than after percutaneous release [r14]. Whether the tendon nodule is the primary lesion or a response to pulley stenosis is not settled in the sources retrieved, so the page shows both structures thickening (clinical model). That steroid injection helps even though the pulley histology is non-inflammatory is not explained by these sources.

structures.name: A1 pulley
structures.effect: Fissured, thinned gliding surface, fibrous replacement and invading vessels; thickened tunnel [r2,r14]

structures.name: Flexor tendon (FDS and FDP)
structures.effect: Thickening or nodule that cannot pass the pulley; thickness decreased after steroid injection [r14]

structures.name: Flexor tendon sheath
structures.effect: Thickened and irritated at the A1 level, which narrows the tunnel (clinical)

structures.name: PIP joint
structures.effect: Fixed flexion contracture in long-standing disease (Quinnell grade 4) [r3]

structures.name: Radial digital nerve (thumb)
structures.effect: Lies over the thumb A1 pulley and is not injured by the disease, but is at risk with release or injection [r1]

muscles.name: Finger flexors (FDS and FDP)
muscles.effect: Forceful grip is painful and catches, so people avoid gripping, and grip strength can fall with disuse and pain (clinical).

muscles.name: Finger extensors and intrinsics
muscles.effect: In a locked digit the extensors cannot free the nodule, so the other hand passively extends the finger (clinical).

muscles.name: Forearm and thenar muscles
muscles.effect: Protective guarding and compensatory overload when the affected digit is spared (clinical).

cellular.description: Repeated forceful flexion raises friction between tendon and pulley surface (clinical model); histology suggests this is a mechanical rather than inflammatory process [r2].
The fibrocartilaginous inner layer fissures and thins [r2].
The inner layer is replaced by fibrous tissue and the vascular outer layer invades the cartilage-like layer; worse changes match worse symptoms [r2].
A thickened tendon segment catches at the narrowed A1 tunnel, producing snapping, then locking [r3].
Steroid injection reduced pulley and tendon thickness [r14]; release divides the pulley so the tendon can glide [r1].

systems.effect: Diabetes raises the odds of trigger finger [r10] and may reduce the response to injection [r13]. Blood glucose can rise after steroid injection, so poorly controlled or insulin-treated patients need monitoring (suggested by the authors of one series) [r3].
Local tenderness at the A1 pulley is the earliest symptom. Pain may be felt along the finger, and at the thumb the radial digital nerve can be irritated by procedures [r3,r1].
Long-standing locking is associated with PIP flexion contracture (Quinnell grade 4), and other hand conditions such as carpal tunnel syndrome can coexist (clinical) [r3].
Repetitive gripping work and vibrating tools are risk settings [r12,r11], so advice must be realistic for the person's job.
Histology was not inflammatory [r2], yet corticosteroid is the standard first-line injection [r5], so the mechanism of benefit remains unclear (clinical comment).

grading.system: Quinnell classification of trigger finger severity (as defined in a large injection series)

grades.description: Tenderness at the A1 pulley only, with no triggering yet [r3].
grades.prognosis: In a series of 715 fingers, 6.4% of grade 1 fingers went on to surgery [r3]
9.5% went on to surgery in the same series [r3]. In another RCT, conservative care succeeded in about 75% of Green grade 1–2 fingers [r6].
16.7% went on to surgery in that series, but the decision was mainly patient preference [r3]. Conservative success was about 60% for Green grade 3 [r6].
12% went on to surgery in the same series [r3]; a fixed contracture usually means a surgical referral (clinical).

timeframes.summary: Trigger finger is a gradual mechanical process without a fixed healing timeline. The phases below are an illustrative clinical model, not drawn from one cited source. Trial follow-up points were 4 weeks for injection in the Cochrane review [r4], 6 weeks for orthosis trials [r7,r6] and 6 months in a release versus injection RCT [r14].

healing.description: Pain at the A1 pulley, occasional snapping; education and load change (clinical)
Frequent triggering or locking; injection or orthosis considered [r5,r7]
Triggering despite injection; repeat injection or release considered [r17,r14]
PIP contracture work, or scar and grip recovery after release; follow the surgeon's protocol (clinical)

milestones.label: Review after corticosteroid injection
milestones.note: The Cochrane review measured treatment success at four weeks (relative risk 3.15 for steroid plus lidocaine versus lidocaine alone) [r4]

milestones.label: End of an orthosis trial
milestones.note: Orthoses were worn for 6 weeks in an RCT, with 60% success for the MCP blocking orthosis [r7]

milestones.label: Decide on repeat injection or release
milestones.note: Outcomes in the orthosis-and-injection trial were reviewed at 6 weeks and 3 months [r6]

milestones.label: Six-month outcome after release or injection
milestones.note: Percutaneous release gave better pain and function than steroid at 6 months in one RCT [r14]

timeframes.returnToSport: Return to forceful gripping work or sport is criteria-based, not time-based: no triggering across 10 repeated forceful fists, pain-free grip and a settled wound after release. Typical timing differs by treatment and by the surgeon's protocol (clinical range).

symptoms: Pain at the base of a finger or thumb in the palm, often worse on gripping
Clicking, catching or snapping as the digit flexes or extends, often worst on waking
Finger locked in flexion that must be freed with the other hand
Stiffness and a feeling of swelling in the palm or finger
Difficulty with fine tasks, gripping tools or holding a steering wheel
Gradual onset, sometimes in several digits, and no single injury
signs: Tenderness over the A1 pulley at the distal palmar crease [r3]
A palpable nodule that moves with the flexor tendon on active flexion (clinical)
Snapping or locking on an active composite fist, and a count of triggering events over 10 fists [r6]
A digit that locks in flexion and straightens with a snap or with passive help [r3]
PIP flexion contracture in long-standing disease [r3]

subjective: Onset, duration and number of digits affected, and which hand is dominant
Pattern of triggering: morning stiffness, snapping only, or locking that needs the other hand
Occupation and hobbies: repetitive gripping, hand-held vibrating tools, tool handle size [r12,r11]
Diabetes (and glycaemic control), thyroid, inflammatory arthritis, and renal disease [r10,r13]
Previous treatment: splint, injection (type and number), surgery, and response
Paraesthesia or night symptoms to screen for carpal tunnel syndrome, which can coexist (clinical)
observation: Resting posture of the digit and any fixed flexion at the PIP joint
Swelling or a visible nodule in the palm
Smooth full fist versus a stuttering fist with one digit lagging
palpation: Tenderness and a nodule over the A1 pulley at the distal palmar crease [r3]
Nodule moving with the tendon as the patient flexes
Other digits, the carpal tunnel and the palmar fascia (for Dupuytren cords) to screen differentials
rangeOfMotion: Active composite fist and full finger extension
Passive extension of a locked finger to separate locking from fixed contracture (Quinnell grade 3 versus 4) [r3]
strength: Grip dynamometry compared with the other hand
Pinch (key, tip and three-point) for trigger thumb
Resisted finger flexion (FDS and FDP tests) to exclude tendon rupture after injection
neuro: Sensation in the median and ulnar digital nerve territories
Phalen or Tinel signs if carpal tunnel symptoms are present (clinical)
functional: Count triggering events during 10 repeated fists [r6]
Observed tool gripping, steering-wheel grip and jar opening
Patient-specific task such as holding a hand tool for 5 minutes (clinical)

specialTests.name: A1 pulley palpation
specialTests.purpose: Locate the pain source at the A1 pulley
specialTests.procedure: Press over the distal palmar crease at the MCP level while the patient slowly flexes and extends the digit.
specialTests.positive: Focal tenderness, sometimes a nodule that moves with the tendon. Tenderness at the A1 pulley only is Quinnell grade 1 [r3].

specialTests.name: Active composite fist (10 repeated fists)
specialTests.purpose: Detect and grade triggering and give a baseline count
specialTests.procedure: The patient makes a full fist and opens it 10 times. Count catching, snapping and locking events.
specialTests.positive: Snapping without locking is grade 2 and snapping with locking is grade 3 [r3]. The number of triggering events in 10 repeated grips was an outcome measure in an RCT [r6].

specialTests.name: Passive extension of a locked digit
specialTests.procedure: When the digit locks in flexion, gently extend it passively at the PIP joint and note whether it releases.
specialTests.positive: A digit that releases passively is locked (grade 3); a digit that cannot be fully extended has a joint contracture (grade 4) [r3].

clinicalRules.name: Diagnosis is clinical
clinicalRules.description: No sensitivity or specificity figures for these examination findings were found in the sources retrieved. Diagnose from the history, A1 tenderness and a catching or locking digit, and exclude the differentials below (clinical).

outcomeMeasures.name: Quinnell grade
outcomeMeasures.use: Severity grading from tenderness to contracture; used in injection and release trials [r3,r14]

outcomeMeasures.name: Number of triggering events in 10 repeated fists
Numeric pain rating scale or visual analogue scale
Grip dynamometry
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective strength compared with the other hand (clinical)

imaging.indication: Typical history, A1 tenderness and triggering
imaging.findings: Imaging is not required for diagnosis (clinical). Ultrasound guidance did not change injection outcomes significantly in a systematic review of RCTs [r17].

imaging.indication: Trauma, suspected arthritis or a fixed contracture
imaging.findings: Excludes fracture, joint degeneration or a bony block (clinical)

imaging.indication: Atypical lump, suspected rupture or suspected infection
imaging.findings: Mass such as a ganglion, tendon or pulley rupture, or fluid in the sheath (clinical)

differentials.name: Boutonnière deformity
differentials.distinguishing: PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension after a central slip injury. There is no snapping and no tenderness at the A1 pulley.

differentials.name: A2 pulley rupture
differentials.distinguishing: An acute pop under a crimp grip, with bowstringing and pain over the proximal phalanx rather than at the MCP crease.

differentials.name: PIP volar plate injury
differentials.distinguishing: Hyperextension injury with PIP swelling and tenderness volarly. There is no snapping at the MCP.

differentials.name: De Quervain's tenosynovitis
differentials.distinguishing: Radial wrist pain over the first dorsal compartment. It may coexist with trigger thumb but does not lock the thumb IP joint.

differentials.name: Dupuytren's contracture
differentials.distinguishing: A palmar nodule or cord and fixed MCP or PIP flexion without snapping. Skin puckering or a visible cord is common.

differentials.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Night paraesthesia in the median nerve digits, not locking. Both conditions can occur together (clinical).

differentials.name: Palmar ganglion or flexor sheath mass
differentials.distinguishing: A discrete lump that may mimic a nodule but does not move with the tendon; ultrasound confirms (clinical).

differentials.name: Infective flexor tenosynovitis
differentials.distinguishing: Hot, swollen finger held flexed with pain on passive extension along the sheath and fever. This is a surgical emergency (clinical).

redFlags: Hot, red, swollen finger held in flexion with pain on passive extension along the sheath, with or without fever: suspect infective flexor tenosynovitis. Refer to emergency the same day (clinical).

Sudden loss of active finger flexion after an injection: suspect flexor tendon rupture. In one paper's literature review, reported complications such as tendon rupture involved triamcinolone doses of 10 mg or more [r3]. Arrange urgent hand surgical review.
Fixed flexion contracture of the PIP joint (grade 4), or triggering that returns after repeated injections: refer to hand surgery [r3].
Poorly controlled or newly suspected diabetes: ask the GP to check glycaemic control. Monitor blood glucose after steroid injection in people with poor control or on insulin [r13,r3].
New numbness at the side of a digit or thumb after injection or release: suspect digital nerve injury. The radial digital nerve crosses the thumb A1 pulley [r1]. Arrange urgent surgical review.
Locked thumb or finger in a young child: refer to a paediatric or hand surgeon for assessment, because release is considered after about 1 year of age [r15].

management.principles: Use shared decision-making between education with activity change, a splint, corticosteroid injection, and release. Corticosteroid injection is a first-line treatment [r12]. Moderate evidence supports injection in the very short term [r5], and the Cochrane review found a relative risk of 3.15 at four weeks for steroid with lidocaine over lidocaine alone, from two small poor-quality trials [r4]. Success is often partial: an older pooled analysis of four RCTs found injection effective in 57% [r9], and a larger insurance-claims analysis reported success rates of 72–73% [r16]. Adding a night orthosis to injection gave no significant benefit in one RCT [r6]. If symptoms persist, release is usually effective, with reported success rates of 90–100% for open release [r1]. Physio interventions have little trial evidence, so measure triggering and pain and review at 4–6 weeks.

medical.name: Corticosteroid injection into the flexor tendon sheath
medical.description: A first-line treatment [r12]. Moderate evidence for a very short-term effect [r5]. Two small Cochrane trials gave relative risk 3.15 (95% CI 1.34–7.40) and a number needed to treat of 3 at four weeks, with no adverse events reported [r4]. Pooled success was 57% in an older review of four RCTs [r9]. Ultrasound-guided versus blind and intra-sheath versus extra-sheath technique did not differ significantly [r17].

medical.name: Choice of steroid (methylprednisolone versus triamcinolone)
medical.description: A systematic review of 13 RCTs pooled remission of 83.6% with methylprednisolone and 44.8% with triamcinolone, but these came from different trials, not head-to-head comparisons. Adverse events (skin atrophy, steroid flare) occurred in 2.8% of triamcinolone patients [r17].

medical.name: Repeat injection after a partial response
medical.description: Second injections improved outcomes in partial responders in the systematic review [r17]. In a Japanese series, 4 mg triamcinolone at intervals of at least 1 month caused no tendon rupture or infection over a median follow-up of 27 months, but the paper's literature review found complications such as tendon rupture only at doses of 10 mg or more [r3].

medical.name: Corticosteroid injection in people with diabetes
medical.description: In one double-blind RCT, injection was significantly less effective in diabetic digits (12 of 19) than non-diabetic digits (25 of 29), and did not reduce surgery compared with placebo [r13]. A claims analysis of 29,722 patients found similar injection success in diabetic (72%) and non-diabetic (73%) patients [r16]. Evidence is conflicting.

medical.name: NSAID injection (diclofenac) as an alternative to steroid
medical.description: In a double-blind RCT of 100 patients, complete resolution at 3 months was 70% with triamcinolone and 53% with diclofenac, and steroid gave quicker relief [r18]. Availability is limited.

medical.name: Percutaneous A1 pulley release
medical.description: In an RCT of 92 people unresponsive to conservative treatment, percutaneous release gave greater pain and functional improvement than steroid injection at 6 months [r14]. A trial cited in a surgical review found no difference in recurrence between open and percutaneous release [r1].

medical.name: Open A1 pulley release
medical.description: Reported success rates are 90–100%. In a larger series of 543 patients, the minor complication rate was 9.6% and the major rate 2.4%, most often persistent stiffness, swelling or pain [r1]. The radial digital nerve at the thumb A1 pulley must be protected.

physio.name: Education and activity modification
physio.description: Explain that the problem is a tendon–pulley mismatch, reduce sustained forceful grip and vibrating tool use, and build up handles. In the orthosis RCT, education, activity modification and tendon gliding exercises were given to everyone as the base program [r7]. No trial tested education alone.

physio.name: MCP joint blocking orthosis
physio.description: In a 6-week RCT of 30 people (Froimson stage 1–3), an MCP blocking orthosis worn full time gave a 60% success rate and significantly greater pain relief than a relative motion orthosis [r7]. Useful for people who prefer to avoid injection.

physio.name: Relative motion extension orthosis
physio.description: Less effective than the MCP blocking orthosis in the same small RCT (success 27% versus 60%) [r7].

physio.name: Routine addition of a night extension orthosis to a corticosteroid injection
physio.description: In a 3-arm RCT of 104 people, adding an orthosis to injection gave no significant benefit at 6 weeks, and overall conservative success was 68.9% [r6]. A systematic review also found splinting as an adjunct had limited impact [r17].

physio.name: Tendon gliding exercises and A1 pulley stretching
physio.description: Flexor tendon gliding exercises were part of the orthosis RCT program [r7], and A1 pulley stretching was part of a Japanese injection protocol [r3]. No trial tested them alone.

physio.name: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT)
physio.description: In a double-blind RCT of 60 people with Quinnell grade 2, high-energy ESWT (4 weekly sessions) gave lower pain and lower QuickDASH than sham at 6 months, whereas low-energy ESWT did not separate from sham [r8]. Single small trial.

education: A trigger finger is a thickened tendon catching in a tight tunnel in the palm. It is common, treatable and not a sign of serious damage.
Injection helps many people, but triggering can return, and diabetes can reduce the response [r9,r13].
Avoid forcing a locked finger open again and again. Reduce sustained tight gripping, use padded or thicker handles, and take breaks from vibrating tools.
If symptoms persist, a small procedure to release the tunnel is usually effective, with a low rate of complications [r1].
Seek urgent help for a hot, swollen finger or a sudden inability to bend the finger after an injection.

rehab.overview: No trial has tested a staged exercise program for trigger finger, so the stages below follow the program elements used in the orthosis RCT (education, activity modification and tendon gliding exercises) [r7] and common clinical convention. Progress by triggering count, pain and grip, not by time. After an injection, avoid excessive gripping for about 1 week (a protocol used in one series) [r3]. After percutaneous or open release, the surgeon's protocol overrides this program.

stages.name: Calm the digit & change the load
stages.timeframe: Weeks 0–3 (and first days after injection or release)
goals: Reduce tenderness and the number of triggering events
precautions: Avoid sustained forceful gripping and vibrating tools
After injection, avoid excessive gripping for about 1 week [r3]
Do not repeatedly force a locked finger open (clinical)
After release, follow the surgeon's wound and motion protocol

exercises.name: MCP blocking orthosis wear
exercises.dosage: Full time for 6 weeks in the RCT [r7]; in practice, adjust to the patient's tasks
exercises.cues: MCP joint held in a blocked position, with the IP joints free to move

exercises.name: Active finger flexion and extension in pain-free range
exercises.cues: Move slowly through the catch without forcing

exercises.name: Gentle passive finger extension (A1 pulley stretch)
exercises.dosage: 5 × 10 s, 3 times daily (clinical convention, used in one protocol [r3])
exercises.cues: Support the MCP joint and extend the fingers to a comfortable stretch

exercises.name: Handle and tool modification
exercises.cues: Use a thicker, padded handle and avoid a tight, sustained pinch

exercises.name: Micro-breaks from gripping work
exercises.dosage: Open and shake the hand every 20–30 minutes (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Alternate tasks and hands where possible

progressionCriteria: Pain with daily tasks 3/10 or less
No signs of infection or tendon rupture

stages.name: Restore glide & range
goals: Full composite fist and full finger extension
PIP extension if a lag is present
precautions: No resisted gripping until triggering has settled
Stop if triggering or pain flares for more than 24 hours (clinical)

exercises.name: Tendon gliding series (straight, hook, full fist, tabletop, straight fist)
exercises.dosage: 5–10 repetitions of each position, 3–4 times daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Move smoothly between positions and hold each for 2–3 s

exercises.name: Differential FDS and FDP glides
exercises.cues: Isolate the PIP and DIP joints while the MCP stays still

exercises.name: Active composite fist and release
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions, 3 times daily; record the number of catches
exercises.cues: Aim for a smooth, full fist

exercises.name: PIP extension stretch with the MCP blocked
exercises.dosage: 5 × 15 s, 3 times daily if an extension lag is present
exercises.cues: Gentle, low-load stretch; avoid pain above 4/10

progressionCriteria: Triggering minimal or absent on 10 fists
Full composite fist and full finger extension
Pain 2/10 or less at rest and with light tasks

stages.name: Grip tolerance & strength
precautions: Regress if triggering returns on 2 consecutive days (clinical convention)
Use built-up handles for sustained gripping tasks

exercises.name: Pinch strengthening with putty
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10 key and tip pinch, 3 times weekly
exercises.cues: Keep the digit smooth through the catch zone

exercises.name: Wrist flexor and extensor strengthening
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–15 with a light dumbbell, 3 times weekly

exercises.name: Graded tool grip with a built-up handle
exercises.dosage: Start at 50% of usual task time and add 10–20% a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Relaxed grip; avoid a white-knuckle squeeze

exercises.name: Farmer carry
exercises.cues: Neutral wrists and a tall posture

progressionCriteria: Grip within about 85–90% of the other hand (clinical convention)
Pain 2/10 or less after loading sessions

prognosis: Many people improve with conservative care, but success is often partial. A pooled analysis of four older RCTs found injection effective in 57% [r9]; in a 3-arm RCT, 68.9% had resolution or improvement with orthosis, injection or both, with success of about 75% for grades 1–2 and 60% for grade 3 on the Green classification [r6]. In a claims analysis of 29,722 patients, injection success was 72–73% regardless of diabetes or sex [r16]. In a Japanese series of 715 fingers, 258 needed only one injection, 457 needed more than one, and 9.8% of patients went on to surgery [r3]. Diabetic digits did worse after injection in a small RCT, with surgery in 7 of 19 versus 3 of 29 non-diabetic digits [r13]. Open release has reported success of 90–100%, with minor complications in 9.6% and major in 2.4% in one large series [r1]. Long-term recurrence after release was not retrieved from the sources used.
prevention: No trial has tested prevention. Reduce sustained forceful gripping and the use of vibrating hand-held tools, which was associated with trigger finger in women [r11] (clinical advice).
Use thicker or padded handles and take breaks from repetitive gripping tasks (clinical).
Good diabetes management is sensible because diabetes raises the odds of trigger finger [r10]. Whether tighter control prevents it was not shown in the sources retrieved.
Treat early tenderness (Quinnell grade 1) with education and load change before triggering develops (clinical).
clinicalPearls: Ask the patient to make 10 fists and count the catches. It grades the problem, guides treatment and gives a baseline for review [r6].
Triggering is usually worst on waking and eases with use. Ask about it, because it can be absent in clinic.
Diabetes changes the odds and may change the response: screen for it and set expectations, but the injection evidence in diabetes conflicts [r13,r16].
An orthosis is a reasonable alternative for those avoiding injection, but adding it to an injection did not help in the RCT [r7,r6].
Do not repeat high-dose steroid injections blindly: reported tendon ruptures involved triamcinolone doses of 10 mg or more in one literature review [r3].
At the thumb, remember the radial digital nerve lies over the A1 pulley when referring for release [r1].

captions.text: A worker grips and swings a hand tool many times a day.
Each firm grip presses the flexor tendons against the pulleys at the base of the fingers.
Repeated loading wears the tendon's gliding surface under the A1 pulley.
Over weeks to months the tunnel and the tendon no longer fit.
Zooming into the base of the finger in the palm.

actions.text: A1 pulley (the usual site of triggering)

actions.label: Grip presses the tendons against the pulley

actions.text: Tendon thickens to form a nodule

captions.text: The flexor tendons run through a sheath held by the A1 pulley at the base of the finger.
Forceful gripping loads the tendons against the pulley.
The flexor tendon thickens to form a nodule.
The pulley's gliding surface wears and the pulley and sheath thicken, narrowing the tunnel.
The nodule catches as it slides under the pulley, so the finger snaps or locks as it straightens.
Tenderness and snapping at the A1 pulley are the classic signs. Release enlarges the tunnel.
Healthy tendon and sheath. The pathology is at the A1 pulley and flexor sheath, shown with a tendon model.
Repeated friction irritates the cells and swells the matrix (a generic tendon-matrix model).
With continued load the matrix becomes disorganised and thickened.
Chronic change: the pulley's gliding surface wears and is replaced by fibrous tissue, not inflammation.
Load change, an orthosis or injection can settle it, but a thickened tunnel may need release.
